470.title: Equal in deeds
470.hook: the four castes are equal before their own deeds
470.howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities ordain people of any background, and seniority among monks and nuns is counted from the day of ordination, not from birth or family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: devaduta, the gray hair a king called a messenger. Your line: the time has come. Now a new week.

This conversation happens after the Buddha has died. His disciple Mahākaccāna, a monk remembered for opening up short teachings at length, is staying in a grove near the city of Madhurā. The king of Madhurā comes to see him with a question that's been circulating. Some brahmins of that time held that their class was the highest: born from Brahmā's own mouth, fair where others were dark, pure where others weren't. What does the monk say to that? Mahākaccāna doesn't answer with a slogan. He asks the king to look at how the world actually works.
screen: `AFTER THE BUDDHA'S DEATH.` → `MAHĀKACCĀNA AT MADHURĀ.` → `IS ONE CLASS THE HIGHEST?`

segments.voice: Society at the time was described in four classes: nobles and warriors, brahmins or priests, merchants, and laborers. Mahākaccāna takes them one test at a time. First, money. If a noble becomes rich, will people of every class rise before him, run his errands, speak pleasantly to win his favor? Yes, says the king. And if a laborer becomes rich? The same. Then in this, the four classes are equal. Second, conduct. If a person of any class kills, steals, lies, what happens after death, as you understand it? Rebirth in a bad state, whatever their class. And if they live well? A good rebirth, whatever their class. Equal again. Third, the law. If a thief is caught breaking into a house, does your court ask his class before punishing him? No. The same punishment for all. Fourth, the spiritual life. If someone of any class shaves their head, goes forth and lives well, do you honor them as a monk? Yes, the king says, whatever their birth. Test after test, the same answer. Mahākaccāna isn't saying everyone is identical, or that background doesn't shape a life. He's saying that when it counts, in what people do and what follows from it, birth doesn't settle anything. At the end, the king asks where the Buddha is now. He has passed away, Mahākaccāna says. And the king goes for refuge to the Buddha who has passed, the teaching, and the community. The teacher was gone; the teaching was still answering questions.

segments.voice: Picture the people you'll meet: someone serving you coffee, someone senior at work, someone sleeping in a doorway, someone in a nice car. Notice any small shift in how you'd greet each one, without scolding yourself. Then picture greeting each with the same eyes and the same voice, and breathe with that.
Vanna. Mahākaccāna's four tests, money, conduct, the law and going forth, and the same answer each time: birth doesn't settle it.
Your line: not by birth. In what people do, the four classes come out equal. That's day four hundred seventy.

471.title: Angulimala, read whole
471.hook: the story from year one, now read in full
471.howItsDone: Angulimāla's verse of truth for a safe birth, the Aṅgulimāla Paritta, is still chanted by monks in Theravada countries for expectant mothers, and his story is told as proof that anyone can change.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vanna, and Mahākaccāna's four tests: money, conduct, the law, going forth. Your line: not by birth.

Pasenadi of Kosala rides out of his capital with five hundred horsemen. His people have been gathering outside the palace, crying out about a killer in the forest, and the king is going to hunt Angulimāla down. On the way, he stops to pay respects to the Buddha. In year one, around day seventy, I told this story in pieces: the road, the chase, I have stopped, the woman in labor, the stones. Now the eighty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, read whole, and quieter scenes like this one come into view.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED HORSEMEN.` → `A KING ON A HUNT.` → `TOLD IN PIECES, NOW READ WHOLE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks him: what's wrong, great king? Is a neighboring kingdom attacking you? No, says Pasenadi. It's a bandit, Angulimāla. I'm going to put him down. Then the Buddha asks an unexpected question. Suppose you saw Angulimāla with his head shaved, in robes, gone forth, gentle, eating one meal a day, keeping the precepts. What would you do? The king says: I'd bow to him, offer him robes and food and shelter, and protect him. But how could someone like that ever become someone like this? The Buddha stretches out his arm and points. There is Angulimāla. The king is terrified, his hair standing on end. Don't be afraid, the Buddha says. You have nothing to fear from him. The king walks over, asks his family name, and offers him robes. Angulimāla says he already has his three. The king turns back to the Buddha and says it plainly: the one we couldn't tame with punishment or weapons, you've tamed without either. And he rides home. The sutta goes on: the woman in labor, the stones on the alms round, and then Angulimāla alone, freed, speaking verses. One is also in the Dhammapada. In Max Müller's words: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." In another verse he says his name had been Harmless, and now, at last, he lives up to it. Read whole, the story isn't only about one man stopping. A king stops too.

Then sit quietly with the picture of the moon coming out from behind a cloud.

Your line: I have stopped. Tamed without punishment or weapons. Day four hundred seventy-one, done.

472.title: Born from the dear
472.hook: a father mad with grief; sorrow comes from what is dear; the king and queen argue it through
472.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers draw on this sutta when helping people with grief, and many Buddhists reflect on the impermanence of loved ones as part of daily practice, alongside loving-kindness toward them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angulimāla, read whole, and a king who rode out to kill and went home. Your line: I have stopped.

This one is about grief, so go gently. A man's only son has died, a small boy. Since then he can't work. He can't eat. He goes to the cremation ground every day and cries out: my only child, where are you? Eventually he comes to the Buddha, who sees at once that something is wrong. Your senses aren't steady, householder. How could they be, he says. My only son is dead. And what the Buddha says next, the man refuses to accept.
screen: `GO GENTLY.` → `MY ONLY CHILD, WHERE ARE YOU?` → `HE REFUSES TO ACCEPT IT.`

segments.voice: So it is, householder, the Buddha says. Sorrow, grief, pain and despair are born from those who are dear. The Pali word is piya, dear, beloved. The father shakes his head. How could that be? Happiness and joy are born from those who are dear. And he walks out, unconvinced. He tells some men playing dice nearby, and they agree with him. The talk travels until it reaches the palace. King Pasenadi hears it and tells Queen Mallikā, and she says: if the Buddha said it, it's so. The king snaps at her: you agree with everything he says, like a pupil with a teacher. So Mallikā sends a messenger to ask the Buddha directly, and he gives more examples, each as raw as the first: a woman whose mother died, who went out of her mind with grief; a man who lost his wife. Then Mallikā does something wise. She doesn't argue in general. She asks the king about his own life. Is our daughter, Princess Vajirī, dear to you? Yes. If anything happened to her, would sorrow arise? Yes, terrible sorrow. And the people of your kingdoms? Am I dear to you? Yes, yes. Then by that, she says, you can see what the Buddha meant. The king rises, turns toward where the Buddha is staying, and pays homage. The sutta never tells anyone to stop loving. It names what comes with love: the grief that waits inside it, born from the same person who is dear.
screen: `PIYA: THE DEAR, THE BELOVED.` · `HAPPINESS, SAYS THE FATHER.` · `MALLIKĀ ASKS ABOUT THEIR DAUGHTER.` · `IT NEVER SAYS STOP LOVING.` · then, large: `THE DEAR BRING GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone very dear to you, alive or gone, and let the warmth of them come first. Then, gently, let in the other side, how it hurts or would hurt to lose them, and let the love and the ache sit side by side, like two hands holding one cup. If it's too much, come back to the breath.
Piya. Sorrow and grief are born from those we love. A grieving father, a queen's question, and a king who finally saw it.
Your line: the dear bring grief. The love is real, and so is the ache inside it. Take care until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 472 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY THE OLD KING BOWS.`

473.title: Why the old king bows
473.hook: King Pasenadi kisses the Buddha's feet and tells why he loves the community
473.howItsDone: Buddhists bow to the Buddha, the teaching and the community, often three times, at shrines, temples and before teachers, and many describe the bow as an expression of gratitude for what they have seen the practice do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: piya, a grieving father, and Queen Mallikā's question. Your line: the dear bring grief.

King Pasenadi again, but much older now. He's out driving through a park, and the trees are quiet and beautiful, the kind of quiet that makes him think of the Buddha. He asks where the Buddha is staying: a fair way off, in a Sakyan town. He goes anyway. At the monastery, he takes off the five signs of a king, the sword, the sunshade, the crown and the rest, and hands them to his general. Then he walks alone to a closed door, coughs, and knocks.
screen: `A QUIET PARK.` → `THE FIVE SIGNS OF A KING, HANDED OVER.` → `A CLOSED DOOR. A KNOCK.`

segments.voice: The Buddha opens the door. And the king of Kosala goes down on the floor, puts his head at the Buddha's feet, kisses them, strokes them, and says his own name: I am Pasenadi, king of Kosala. The Buddha asks, why such honor? The king tells him, reason after reason. I see your monks living together in harmony, like milk and water, looking at one another with kind eyes. I don't always see that, he says, even among brothers and sisters. I sit in judgment in my own court, and people interrupt me. When you teach hundreds of people, there isn't a sound. Once someone coughed, and the person beside him nudged him: quiet, the Teacher is speaking. Clever people come to trap you with questions, and leave as your followers. My own two chamberlains, men I feed and pay, lie with their heads toward you at night, and their feet toward me. Then the most personal one. The Buddha is a noble, and so am I. He's of Kosala, and so am I. He's eighty, and so am I. That's why I bow. After the king leaves, the Buddha calls these the king's monuments to the Dhamma, and tells the monks to learn them. A king listing, not miracles or doctrines, but behavior: how monks look at each other, how a room stays quiet, where servants point their heads. The commentaries add a sadder frame. While the king was inside, his general rode off with the royal insignia, and Pasenadi never sat on his throne again. Which makes his last reason, both of us are eighty, all the more tender.

segments.voice: Ask yourself, like the king, what you've actually seen in your own life that makes this path worth walking: not a doctrine, but something noticed, a calmer morning, a kinder reply, a person whose way of living moved you. Dhammacetiya. Pasenadi, at eighty, kisses the Buddha's feet and gives his reasons: harmony, quiet, and things he'd seen with his own eyes.
Your line: why I bow. His reasons were things he'd seen, not things he'd heard. See you tomorrow.

474.title: Watching him walk
474.hook: the old brahmin's pupil follows the Buddha for months, watching how he walks and eats
474.howItsDone: Monastic training in Buddhist traditions gives careful attention to deportment, how to walk, sit, eat and wear robes, and lay Buddhists often say they learned most from watching how a respected teacher lives day to day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammacetiya, and an old king's reasons for bowing, all things he'd seen. Your line: why I bow.

How do you really get to know someone? Not their profile, not their speeches. You watch them on an ordinary day: how they treat a waiter, how they eat when they think nobody's looking. In the city of Mithilā lives a famous brahmin named Brahmāyu, a master of the old Vedic learning, and the sutta says he's a hundred and twenty years old. He hears the Buddha is nearby, and he does something careful. He sends his best student, a young man named Uttara, to watch. Not to debate. To watch.
screen: `WATCH THEM ON AN ORDINARY DAY.` → `BRAHMĀYU, A HUNDRED AND TWENTY.` → `NOT TO DEBATE. TO WATCH.`

segments.voice: Uttara follows the Buddha for seven months, the sutta says, like a shadow that never leaves. Then he goes home and reports, down to the smallest movement. When he walks, he steps off with the right foot. His stride is neither too long nor too short, neither too fast nor too slow. His knees and ankles don't knock together. When he looks back, he turns his whole body, the way an elephant does. When he sits down in a house, he doesn't drop into the seat or fidget once he's there. When he eats, he takes rice and curry in proportion, and turns each mouthful over two or three times before swallowing. He tastes the food, the report says, but without greed for the taste. After eating he sits in silence for a while, then gives a blessing for the meal, and he doesn't find fault with the food. When he teaches, his voice is clear and carries exactly as far as the gathering, and no farther. And so it goes: robes, bowl, washing, sleeping. Notice what convinces Uttara. Not an argument. Not a wonder. A man who is the same in the kitchen as on the teaching seat. Brahmāyu hears the report, bows in the Buddha's direction, and later goes to meet him. The sutta says he understood the teaching that day and died not long after. A hundred and twenty years old, and what first reached him was a description of someone eating rice.
screen: `SEVEN MONTHS, LIKE A SHADOW.` · `RIGHT FOOT FIRST, NEITHER FAST NOR SLOW.` · `TASTE WITHOUT GREED.` · `THE SAME IN THE KITCHEN AS ON THE SEAT.` · then, large: `WATCH HOW THEY WALK.`

segments.voice: Picture someone whose goodness you trust, not for what they say but for how they are, doing something ordinary: walking into a room, eating, answering a phone. Notice what you see. Then, for the rest of the sit, turn the same quiet attention on yourself: how you're sitting, how you're breathing, right now.
Iriyapatha. Uttara followed the Buddha for seven months and reported how he walked, sat and ate. What convinced him was the ordinary.
Your line: watch how they walk. Goodness shows in the kitchen as much as on the teaching seat. Day four hundred seventy-four, done.

475.title: Any wood makes fire
475.hook: a young brahmin argues caste; fire from any wood burns the same
475.howItsDone: Buddhist communities ordain people of every background, and teachers in South Asia, including the movement led by B. R. Ambedkar, have drawn on suttas like this one in rejecting discrimination by birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: iriyapatha, and what seven months of watching revealed. Your line: watch how they walk.

Five hundred brahmins are staying in Sāvatthī, and they're worried. This Gotama is teaching that all four classes can be purified. Someone has to go and argue with him. They choose Assalāyana, sixteen years old, brilliant, already a master of the old texts. He doesn't want to go. The Buddha speaks the Dhamma, he says, and someone who does is hard to argue with. They insist: don't be beaten without a fight. So a sixteen-year-old walks in to debate the Buddha, carrying his elders' claim on his shoulders.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED WORRIED BRAHMINS.` → `ASSALĀYANA, SIXTEEN.` → `DON'T BE BEATEN WITHOUT A FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Assalāyana states the claim as the brahmins of that time held it: brahmins are the highest class, born of Brahmā, from his mouth. The Buddha's first answer is almost blunt. Brahmin women are seen menstruating, pregnant, giving birth and nursing. Brahmins are born from wombs like everyone else. Then he widens the view. In the lands to the northwest, among the Greeks and Kambojans, there are only two classes, masters and servants, and people move from one to the other. So the four-class order isn't a law of nature. Then gentler tests. Can only a brahmin develop a mind of loving-kindness? No, all four classes can. Can only a brahmin take a back scrubber and bath powder to the river and get clean? No, anyone can. And then the fire. Suppose, the Buddha says, a king gathers a hundred men of different births. Those of high birth make fire with fine woods: sal, pine, lotus, sandalwood. Those of low birth use scraps from a dog's trough, a pig's trough, a washerman's tub, castor-oil wood. Would one fire have flame and color and light, and the other not? Would one cook food and the other not? No, Assalāyana admits. Fire is fire. Whatever the wood, it burns the same and gives the same heat. By the end the young man sits silent, head bowed, and goes for refuge. The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "I do not call a man a Brâhmana because of his origin or of his mother." In the Buddhist texts, the word is kept, and given to conduct.

476.title: Preserving truth
476.hook: say "this is my belief", not "only this is true"
476.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite this sutta, with the Kālāma Sutta, when encouraging students to hold teachings honestly, saying what they believe and why, and to verify through practice rather than insist on being right.

segments.voice: Yesterday: aggi. Sandalwood or a pig's trough, the same light and heat. Your line: fire is fire. Today closes a week.

Another sixteen-year-old brahmin, another tone entirely. His name is Kāpaṭhika, and he's sitting in a crowd around the Buddha with his elders, including the wealthy brahmin Caṅkī. He keeps interrupting. The Buddha asks him to wait until the elders have finished. Caṅkī speaks up for him: he's learned, he can hold his own in a discussion. So the Buddha turns to him, and Kāpaṭhika asks a real question. Our ancient hymns, he says, have been handed down for generations, and about them we brahmins conclude: only this is true, anything else is wrong. What do you say to that?
screen: `KĀPAṬHIKA, SIXTEEN.` → `CAṄKĪ SPEAKS UP FOR HIM.` → `ONLY THIS IS TRUE?`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks him: is there a single brahmin, now or in the past seven generations of teachers, who says, I know this, I see this: only this is true? No, Kāpaṭhika admits. Then, the Buddha says, it's like a line of blind people, each holding the one in front. The first doesn't see, the middle doesn't see, the last doesn't see. Then he names five ways people come to hold things: faith, liking, tradition, careful reasoning, and a view that seems right after reflection. Each of these, he says, can turn out two ways. Something deeply believed can be empty and false; something not believed at all can be true. So how does a person preserve the truth? If a person has faith, they preserve the truth when they say: this is my faith. And they don't go further, to the conclusion: only this is true, everything else is wrong. The same with liking, tradition, reasoning: this is what I've received, this is how I reason. Said that way, the truth is kept safe. The Buddha doesn't tell Kāpaṭhika to drop his hymns. He tells him how to hold them honestly. The sutta then goes on to discovering truth, and finally arriving at it, through long practice. But the first step is simply this way of speaking: say what you believe, and how you came to it. That leaves room for the person across the table to do the same.
